context: The iPhone app needs visibility into distributed mission state without becoming a new authority boundary before Qubes worker semantics are proven.

approaches.name: read-only HTTPS snapshot client
approaches.correctness: strong separation: phone observes state but cannot mutate workers
approaches.robustness: fail-closed on non-HTTPS, malformed response, non-2xx, or missing revision
approaches.resourceUse: low; no persistent socket or background daemon
approaches.qa: requires Swift build plus server contract tests once /api/missions is implemented

approaches.name: bidirectional command API from iPhone
approaches.correctness: weaker at this stage because it creates a second mutation/authentication path
approaches.robustness: requires nonce, replay, authorization, reconciliation, and command fencing
approaches.latency: low interactive latency but higher protocol complexity
approaches.qa: deferred until worker boundary is REAL-WORKER READY

approaches.name: persistent websocket control plane
approaches.correctness: good eventual UX but adds ordering/reconnect semantics
approaches.robustness: requires durable cursor and reconnect reconciliation

winnerReason: The read-only snapshot client gives immediate owner visibility with the smallest authority surface, resource footprint, and regression risk. It preserves the existing durable coordinator as the sole mutation authority.
failuresAndLessons: Do not expose mission mutation from the phone merely for UI convenience.
A telemetry response needs a revision so stale or reordered snapshots can be detected when the server contract is implemented.
Transport security alone is not sufficient for future command mutations; those must reuse durable request identity and replay/fencing semantics.
nextGate: Implement a read-only /api/missions contract backed by a safe mission snapshot source, add Node contract tests, then compile/test the Swift client.
